Chain Care on the Road

A motorcycle chain is a wearing component that demands regular attention, especially on tour when you are covering hundreds of miles daily. A poorly maintained chain wears faster, robs power, can snap at speed, and damages expensive sprockets. Taking five minutes to clean and lubricate your chain every evening is one of the best investments in reliability you can make.

How Often to Lube on Tour

As a general rule, lubricate your chain every 300-500 miles during a tour, or whenever it looks dry. In wet conditions, lube more frequently as rain washes lubricant off faster. After any rain ride, clean and re-lube the chain at your next stop.

Essential Chain Tools for Touring

  • Chain lube — A small can of quality chain lube. Motul Chain Lube Road, Putoline Chain Spray, or Bel-Ray Blue Tac are all excellent options. Choose a road-specific lube rather than off-road which flings off at speed.
  • Chain cleaner — A small bottle of chain cleaner or degreaser removes old lube and grime before re-application. Muc-Off Chain Cleaner is popular and effective.
  • Chain brush — A three-sided chain brush cleans the chain quickly without damaging O-ring seals. Available for a few pounds from any motorcycle shop.
  • Latex gloves — Disposable gloves keep your hands clean during chain maintenance. Pack a few pairs in your toolkit.

Chain Maintenance Technique

Step 1: Put the bike on its centre stand or paddock stand. If neither is available, push the bike forward in neutral while working on sections of chain.

Step 2: Spray chain cleaner on the lower run of the chain and scrub with the chain brush. Work around the entire chain.

Step 3: Wipe the chain dry with a rag.

Step 4: Apply chain lube to the inside of the lower chain run while rotating the wheel. The centrifugal force distributes lube to the outside as you ride.

Step 5: Check chain tension according to your owner's manual specification. Adjust if necessary.

Never use WD-40 or other penetrating oils as chain lubricant. They wash the factory grease out of the O-ring seals, dramatically reducing chain life. Always use motorcycle-specific chain lube designed for O-ring or X-ring chains.

Checking Chain Wear

A worn chain is dangerous. Pull the chain away from the rear sprocket — if you can see daylight between the chain and sprocket teeth, the chain needs replacement. A chain wear tool gives a precise measurement. Never replace the chain without also replacing both sprockets, as a new chain on worn sprockets will accelerate wear dramatically.
keyTakeaways: Lubricate every 300 to 500 miles on tour, and more often in the wet as rain washes lube off.
Use a road-specific chain lube, not off-road lube which flings off at speed.
Never use WD-40 as chain lube; it strips the grease from the O-ring seals.
Apply lube to the inside of the lower chain run while rotating the wheel, then let it settle.
Replace the chain and both sprockets together, never a new chain on worn sprockets.

faq.q: How often should I lube the chain on tour?
faq.a: As a general rule, lubricate every 300 to 500 miles or whenever the chain looks dry. In wet conditions, lube more frequently because rain washes the lubricant off faster, and always clean and re-lube after a rain ride at your next stop. A quick evening check and lube is one of the best reliability habits you can build on a long tour.

faq.q: Can I use WD-40 or GT85 as chain lube?
faq.a: No. Penetrating oils like WD-40 wash the factory grease out of the O-ring or X-ring seals, dramatically reducing chain life. Always use a motorcycle-specific chain lube designed for sealed chains. A light spray of WD-40 can be used to clean a very grimy chain before proper lubing, but it must never be the lubricant itself.

faq.q: What is the correct way to apply chain lube?
faq.a: Clean the chain first with cleaner and a three-sided brush, then wipe it dry. Apply lube to the inside of the lower chain run while slowly rotating the rear wheel, so centrifugal force distributes it outward as you ride. Let it settle for a few minutes before riding off, which stops it flinging straight onto your wheel.

faq.q: How do I know when the chain needs replacing?
faq.a: Pull the chain away from the rear sprocket. If you can see daylight between the chain and the sprocket teeth, it is worn and needs replacing. A chain wear tool gives a precise measurement. A worn chain is dangerous and can snap at speed, so do not put off replacement once it shows significant wear.

faq.q: Do I need to replace the sprockets too?
faq.a: Yes, always replace the chain and both sprockets as a set. Fitting a new chain to worn sprockets accelerates wear dramatically, because the hooked, pointed teeth of an old sprocket chew through fresh chain quickly. Replacing all three together costs more upfront but gives full mileage from the new components.
